title: Competitor flipbook: answers for shared vs dedicated inference
content:
Purpose
This is a compact flipbook for AE/SEs and procurement leads when the buyer is evaluating shared (multi-tenant) managed endpoints versus Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pools). Focus: short soundbites, objection responses, and procurement asks tied to SLA, isolation, predictable throughput, and commercial tradeoffs.

Structure
- One-liners for execs
- Quick counters (what buyers say / how we respond)
- Procurement checklist (must-have clauses + optional asks)
- Tactical negotiation play (concessions that keep margin while addressing buyer needs)
- Technical backup notes for SEs

One-liners (elevator)
- For Platform Leads: "Dedicated capacity means you pay for predictability, not per-request volatility — guaranteed GPU slices, no noisy neighbors, and measurable P99 latency under your workload profile."
- For Legal/Security: "We offer a private tenant surface: customer-only compute, KMS integration, and audit trails for all inference requests."
- For Finance: "Reserved capacity converts variable token spend into predictable monthly commitments with built-in headroom for spikes — easier forecasting and volume-backed unit economics."

Buyer objection / AE response (short)
Q: "Why not just use the cloud provider’s managed endpoints?"
A: "Managed endpoints are convenient but optimized for generality. Redwood Dedicated is built specifically for LLM inference: GPU-optimized runtime, continuous batching and KV-cache efficiency, and routing controls that keep P99 latency within your SLOs at scale. Put simply: better cost-per-effective-inference and fewer production incidents when demand is steady."

Q: "Can’t we get similar isolation with VPC peering on shared infra?"
A: "Network isolation is only part of the story. Our Dedicated model isolates GPU compute and scheduling — that removes noisy neighbor interference at the hardware/allocator level, which is the root cause of tail latency and throughput variability."

Q: "What if our load is spiky?"
A: "We combine dedicated baseline capacity for predictability and burst credits for short-term spikes. Procurement can choose a burst policy (minutes of headroom) or an autoscale band. The key is that baseline capacity protects your 99th percentile SLAs while burst covers temporary surges."

Procurement checklist (must-have clauses)
- SLA: uptime for inference control plane (monthly %), plus throughput SLOs for reserved capacity measured by model family and sequence-length bucket (e.g., 8k tokens at target QPS)
- Tail latency target: define P95/P99 targets with testing harness (customer prompt set) and remediation credits if missed
- Isolation guarantee: physical GPU pool reservation clause and statement of non-shared GPU tenancy for covered instances
- Capacity reservation & elasticity: committed baseline GPU-hours + documented burst policy (minutes/hours of scalable headroom)
- RTO/RPO for control plane: control plane failover commitments and customer data snapshot cadence
- Pricing/overage: hourly rate for burst consumption, formula for sustained overage conversion to committed capacity
- Migration & portability: exportable KV cache / model pinning and rollback procedure in case of deprovisioning
- Security: KMS/HSM integration, SOC/ISO attestations, optional on-prem bundle for air-gapped deployments

Optional procurement asks to push for (high probability wins)
- Pilot SLA credits: small credit pool (one quarter’s consumption) tied to pilot performance verification
- Early termination mutual exit path only for specific non-performance triggers (don’t give away general termination rights)
- Price protection for first 12 months tied to committed GPU-hours
- Joint load-testing window and acceptance criteria (use buyer prompt set and our trace + perf dashboard)

Tactical negotiation play (what to concede vs keep)
- Concede: a bounded trial with measured credits; offer 1–2 weeks of burst credits to prove steady-state economics. This buys trust without eroding committed ARR.
- Hold firm: isolation guarantee and measurable throughput SLOs — these are core product differentiators and operationally costly if overloaded.
- Concede: limited security review sandbox access for procurement/legal teams to run compliance scans.
- Hold firm: migration mechanics — customer must run acceptance tests before conversion of pilot to committed contract; avoid open-ended portability guarantees that leak engineering effort.

Competitive counters (soundbites)
- Versus public cloud managed endpoints: "They give you an endpoint; we guarantee an inferred cost and latency envelope at production scale."
- Versus self-hosted open-source runtimes: "Self-hosting buys control but costs ops cycles, unexpected regressions, and longer time-to-market. Redwood bundles the runtime, telemetry, and on-call runbook so your engineers ship features, not infra fixes."
- Versus other inference platforms: "We prioritize production economics — not raw peak throughput. Our suggestions (batching, quant profiles, KV cache) are prescriptive and tied to observable unit-cost gains for your workloads."

SE technical notes (for deeper buyer Qs)
- Runtime specifics to highlight: continuous batching, shard-aware KV cache eviction, dynamic kernel selection per model/seq-len, and quantization profiles optimized by model family. These combine to lower P50/P95 costs and keep P99 stable.
- Measurement strategy: always validate SLAs on buyer prompt sets and token distributions. Synthetic benchmarks are noisy; we require a representative workload for contract measurement.
- Failover behavior: Dedicated capacity includes automatic fallback to nearline variants (lower-throughput/cheaper models) with configurable circuit-breaker policies. This prevents total service outages during regional incidents.

SLA measurement example (engineer-friendly)
- Define buckets: small (<512 tokens), medium (512-2048), large (2048-8192)
- Baseline test: 1-hour steady-state test at negotiated QPS per bucket using buyer prompts
- Metrics emitted: request latency (P50/P95/P99), success rate (% non-error), GPU occupancy, per-token egress cost estimate
- Credit policy: missed monthly P99 target => service credit = min(25% of monthly committed fees, proportional to measured shortfall)

Sample objection rebuts (scripted)
- Buyer: "We’re worried about vendor lock-in."
  Response: "We publish model variant specs, exportable KV caches, and a documented rollback plan. Lock-in risk is lower when you evaluate total cost of ownership: the months your team spends firefighting infra and re-tuning models are real costs."
- Buyer: "How do we know your dedicated pool won’t be oversubscribed?"
  Response: "Capacity is machine-reserved and mapped to contracts. Our scheduling avoids oversubscription on reserved slices; we operate a separate allocation plane for reserved customers, and we publish utilization dashboards during onboarding."

Quick negotiation checklist for AE/SE before contract hand-off
- Gather buyer prompt set and 1-week telemetry sample (if available)
- Propose baseline GPU-hours and burst credit policy tuned to historical QPS and peak-to-average ratio
- Define acceptance test plan and SLAs with measurable, automated evidence export
- Flag legal for isolation wording and KMS integration; run security questionnaire early

Appendix: example short SLA clause (talking language for legal)
"Redwood will provide Dedicated Capacity that is reserved for Customer use and is not shared with other customers for the duration of the Agreement. Redwood shall make best commercially reasonable efforts to maintain a monthly P99 inference latency not to exceed the agreed threshold for the agreed model and token bucket. If Redwood fails to meet the monthly P99 target as measured against the Customer’s accepted test harness, Customer will be eligible for service credits equal to a percentage of that month’s committed fees, as specified in Schedule A."

What success looks like for a buyer pilot (operational milestones)
1) Baseline run: 1 week of production traffic routed to dedicated pool with real prompts
2) Performance verification: P99 within target in >27 of 30 days window during pilot
3) Cost confirmation: per-effective-inference cost within expected band (±15%)
4) Security sign-off: KMS and audit logs validated by buyer security team

Notes to SEs: keep the pilot constrained and instrumented. Ask for the prompt set early and calibrate batching/Q-profile before ramping traffic. Use the acceptance test to close procurement objections quickly.

End of flipbook
This doc is intentionally short and practical — keep it on the AE/SE tablet during procurement calls. Update the soundbites after every lost deal to capture fresh objections.
